## Paper

## Abstract

Antiferroelectric two-dimensional materials, with their unique physical mechanisms, exhibit tunable polarization dynamics and layered structural characteristics, enabling the synergistic implementation of synaptic plasticity, sensory-mimetic functionality, and in-memory computing within a unified device architecture. These capabilities meet the growing polymorphic requirements of neuromorphic systems and position such materials as strong candidates for next-generation neuromorphic computing platforms. Among them, CuBiP₂Se₆ stands out among 2D antiferroelectric materials due to its intrinsic antiferroelectric properties, featuring a stable interlayer antiparallel Cu⁺ dipole configuration. This structure, combined with its relaxor-like behavior, enables a reversible transition between antiferroelectric and ferroelectric states under an applied electric field, along with gradual polarization tuning. This transition mechanism enables continuously tunable conductance states, providing essential physical support for the gradual modulation of synaptic weights and the hardware implementation of complex neural functions, making it particularly suited for high-precision emulation of multilevel synaptic plasticity in neuromorphic applications. In this work, memristor based on two-dimensional antiferroelectric CuBiP₂Se₆ exhibit stable multilevel conductance states, high endurance, and excellent device uniformity, thus supporting diverse neurosynaptic functions and advanced learning rules. These attributes highlight the immense potential of antiferroelectric 2D materials as a foundation for compact, energy-efficient, and highly integrated neuromorphic hardware.

---

## Introduction

The surging demand for energy-efficient, multifunctional computing power has revealed the limitations of traditional von Neumann architectures, notably serial processing and escalating power dissipation1–6. As a result, neuromorphic computing, which is modeled on the parallel and low-information processing of the brain, has come to the forefront7,8. Next-generation neuromorphic systems require hardware capable of emulating complex biological learning rules and supporting a broad spectrum of synaptic functions9–14. While memristors have advanced in-memory and compute-in-memory architectures by leveraging their analog and nonvolatile resistive switching, most current devices- as illustrated in Fig. 1a are limited to first-order synaptic dynamics, such as short-term plasticity (STP) and basic spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)15–18. Although STDP circuits excel at certain tasks, their reinforcement-based nature restricts synaptic stability and adaptability, making them inadequate for capturing the richer temporal and rate-based synaptic modulation observed in biological systems19.

To address these challenges, materials and device platforms must go beyond simple Hebbian learning, enabling history-dependent, nonlinear, and homeostatic plasticity like BCM (Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro) learning20–33. Among them, the BCM rule17,34 represents a rate-based synaptic plasticity model that extends the classical Hebbian paradigm by introducing the average postsynaptic firing rate as a regulatory factor, thereby enabling synaptic weight updates to reflect the historical activity of the neuron (Fig. 1b). Theoretically, the time-dependent dynamic processes inherent in physical mechanisms such as ion migration and trap-state modulation offer promising avenues for implementing history-dependent and nonlinearly evolving weight updates required by the BCM rule24–26,30. However, the practical realization of BCM-compatible behavior and the required multifunctional synaptic modulation at the device level still faces considerable challenges, such as unstable conductive pathways, poor performance uniformity, limited reproducibility, and insufficient endurance. These issues are primarily attributed to the immaturity of material systems, the high complexity of multifunctional integration, and the challenges associated with device fabrication processes.

Compared with conventional ferroelectric (FE) systems, antiferroelectric (AFE) materials—with their near-zero remanent polarization and antiparallel dipole configurations—can achieve analog, continuously tunable conductance modulation, making them ideal candidates for energy-efficient neuromorphic devices35–39. Their unique polarization-switching mechanism further endows them with higher breakdown fields36,40, faster polarization switching speeds41,42, lower energy dissipation36,43, and excellent fatigue resistance44,45. In particular, relaxor-type AFE materials exhibit gradual polarization responses under external electric fields and slowly relax back once the field is removed46,47. Such dynamical characteristics more closely resemble the time-dependent and history-sensitive behaviors of biological synapses, rendering them especially suitable for hardware implementation of sliding-threshold regulation in BCM-type plasticity.

To the best of our knowledge, the van der Waals layered compound CuBiP₂Se₆ (CBPS) is the first 2D AFE semiconductor and have outstanding properties: it possesses intrinsic antiferroelectric order with antiparallel dipoles, enabling nonlinear, history-dependent, and analog conductance modulation. Furthermore, its dangling-bond-free surfaces and atomically thin geometry ensure excellent interfacial quality, scalability, and compatibility with silicon-based CMOS technologies48–52, distinguishing CBPS as a promising platform for mimicking complex synaptic functionalities in neuromorphic applications.

In this work, we report a vertical memristor array based on 2D relaxor AFE CBPS. The devices exhibit robust multilevel conductance modulation, stable bipolar switching (sustaining over 1000 cycles), and an overall yield exceeding 90%, reflecting high process reproducibility. Neuromorphic functionalities include paired-pulse facilitation, long-term potentiation/depression, and, through triplet-STDP pulse protocols, device-level manifestation of frequency-dependent weight updates and a sliding plasticity threshold effectively mimics key aspects of BCM learning, enabling advanced forms of synaptic plasticity crucial for adaptive information processing. In addition, the devices demonstrate electrically driven nociceptor-like responses, responding sharply to suprathreshold inputs; this is analogous to how biological systems prioritize the rapid transmission of critical or potentially harmful sensory information. The integration of both BCM-type learning and nociceptive response in a single device reflects the polymorphic nature required for robust neuromorphic computing. Leveraging these dynamic synaptic features, device characteristics were mapped into an artificial neural network for facial recognition. The advanced synaptic plasticity empowered by BCM learning, together with the adaptive sensitivity derived from nociceptor-like response, jointly contribute to more effective feature extraction and information discrimination within the neural network. As a result, the system achieves a classification accuracy exceeding 90%, demonstrating not only excellent trainability but also the practical value of integrating diverse synaptic behaviors within neuromorphic hardware for next-generation artificial intelligence applications. This work establishes antiferroelectric 2D materials—specifically CBPS—as a powerful platform for polymorphic neuromorphic devices, combining fine-tuned and reliable synaptic emulation with CMOS compatibility and integration potential. These advances mark a significant step toward energy-efficient, highly adaptive brain-inspired hardware that can tackle the increasingly complex demands of future computing systems.

---

## Results

The crystal structure of CBPS is illustrated in Fig. 1c (top view) and Fig. 1e (side view). To verify the chemical composition and structural integrity of the synthesized CBPS single crystals, comprehensive characterizations were conducted, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealed a molar ratio of Cu, Bi, P, and Se close to 1:1:2:6, in good agreement with the theoretical stoichiometry of CBPS, confirming successful synthesis of the target compound. Elemental mapping further demonstrated uniform spatial distribution of the constituent elements across the nanosheet, without apparent aggregation or depletion, indicating excellent compositional homogeneity. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images, as shown in Fig. 1d, reveal well-aligned lattice fringes with no observable structural defects, indicating high crystal quality and a layered structure. In addition, the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern displays sharp and well-defined diffraction spots with hexagonal symmetry, further confirming the single-crystalline nature of the CBPS flakes (Supplementary Fig. 2). In addition, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern displayed in Supplementary Fig. 2 shows sharp and well-defined diffraction peaks that match well with the standard CBPS pattern, further confirming the phase purity and structural consistency of the material. The Raman spectrum of CBPS, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3, exhibits several characteristic peaks at 111.7, 135.3, 207.5, 431.9, and 465.9 cm⁻¹. According to previous reports47,53–55, the low-frequency peaks at 111.7 and 135.3 cm⁻¹ are associated with lattice vibrations involving Bi-Se and Cu-Se bonds, while the dominant peak at 207.5 cm⁻¹ is attributed to the symmetric stretching vibration of the [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ unit. The higher-frequency peaks at 431.9 and 465.9 cm⁻¹ correspond to the P-Se bond stretching vibrations within the [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ group. Based on symmetry considerations, the peaks labeled in red represent out-of-plane modes, whereas those in blue correspond to in-plane modes. At room temperature, CBPS exhibits distinct AFE behavior. First-principles calculations by Reimers et al.46,47 suggest that CBPS consists of layered [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ anionic frameworks interleaved with Cu⁺ and Bi³⁺ cations. Cu⁺ ions typically occupy octahedral sites, but due to their small ionic radius and weak coordination bonding, they tend to shift either vertically or laterally53 (Supplementary Fig. 4). These displacements modulate the local coordination environment, thereby tuning the polarization state and enabling electric-field-induced transitions between FE and AFE phases. When Cu⁺ ions displace vertically, local dipoles are formed. If adjacent layers exhibit opposite displacement directions, the resulting interlayer dipoles cancel out, leading to near-zero net polarization—a hallmark of AFE order.

Under a sufficiently strong electric field, the Cu⁺ ions align in the same direction, generating net polarization and inducing a transition from AFE to FE state, as illustrated in the schematic in Fig. 1e. This transition is typically accompanied by pronounced polarization responses. The AFE nature of CBPS was further validated by polarization-electric field (P-E) hysteresis measurements. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, the optical microscopy image and atomic force microscopy (AFM) scan reveal a ~20 nm-thick CBPS flake uniformly bridging the crossbar electrodes, ensuring a stable interface for electrical characterization. As shown in Fig. 1f, the device exhibits a characteristic double-loop P-E profile under an applied electric field. Unlike classical AFE materials that undergo abrupt polarization switching, CBPS shows smooth and gradual P-E loops, indicating a relaxor response. This behavior is attributed to the progressive alignment of initially disordered polar nanoregions under the electric field, a signature of relaxor AFE materials56,57. Furthermore, typical relaxor antiferroelectric features were consistently observed across a wide temperature range (210−330 K) and in devices with different thicknesses, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 6-7. This process was further corroborated by piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) analysis. As shown in Fig. 1g, the PFM phase signal becomes increasingly pronounced upon continuous electrical stimulation, indicating electric-field-induced domain reorientation. In parallel, the corresponding PFM amplitude mapping shows a significant enhancement in signal intensity, reflecting a progressive increase in local piezoelectric response. These observations are consistent with the accumulation of aligned dipoles and confirm the presence of electric-field-driven domain evolution in CBPS. The characterization results confirm that the synthesized CBPS crystals exhibit a well-ordered layered structure, high crystallinity, and uniform composition. Their relaxor AFE behavior with smooth, tunable polarization and reversible transitions provides a reliable basis for CBPS-based memristor design and neuromorphic applications.

A vertical 5 × 5 memristor array was fabricated using the two-dimensional relaxor antiferroelectric material CBPS as the active layer, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2a, with the optical image shown in Supplementary Fig. 8. Electrical measurements reveal that the device exhibits clear bipolar resistive switching under ±1.5 V voltage sweeps (Fig. 2b), which can be attributed to field-driven vertical Cu⁺ ion displacement and the associated polarization modulation. A compliance current of 100 μA was applied during testing to avoid over-current damage, and the high-resistance state (HRS) and low-resistance state (LRS) values were consistently extracted at a reading voltage of 0.5 V. Under these conditions, the device maintains a high ON/OFF conductance ratio (>10²) over 1000 consecutive switching cycles without performance degradation, demonstrating excellent endurance. The statistical distribution of HRS and LRS values over 1000 cycles, presented in Supplementary Fig. 9, together with the consecutive I–V switching characteristics of the CBPS-based memristor that remain stable even after 100 days (Supplementary Fig. 10) further confirms the stability and reproducibility of the resistive switching behavior. These results highlight that the layered crystal structure and antipolar configuration of CBPS enable robust and reversible switching characteristics. Additionally, the fabricated 5 × 5 array exhibited a device yield of 92% (23 out of 25 devices), which successfully demonstrated stable neuromorphic behaviors, including nonlinear current–voltage characteristics and reliable multi-pulse conductance responses (Supplementary Fig. 11-12), confirming the device’s reliability and compatibility with large-scale integration. Short-term synaptic plasticity characteristics were evaluated by applying paired voltage pulses (3 V, 20 ms) with varying inter-pulse intervals (Δt = 20–500 ms). As depicted in Fig. 2c, the second excitatory postsynaptic current (A₂) consistently exceeds the first (A₁), and the PPF index (A₂/A₁ × 100%) decays exponentially with increasing interval, closely emulating neurotransmitter residual effects observed in biological synapses.

The synaptic weight modulation was further investigated by tuning the pulse amplitude, number, and width. When increasing the write voltage from 3 V to 8 V under otherwise identical conditions (20 pulses, 20 ms interval), the device exhibits a stepwise increase in conductance under a non-destructive read voltage of 0.5 V (Fig. 2d). The inset highlights a cumulative increase in current with stronger electric fields, indicating enhanced Cu⁺ displacement and dipole alignment. Under fixed pulse conditions (3 V, 20 ms), the conductance increases progressively with pulse number (10, 20, 50) and saturates at higher levels (Fig. 2e), revealing a characteristic accumulation effect. Pulse width also plays a significant role: extending the duration from 1 ms to 40 ms results in notably higher conductance (Supplementary Fig. 13), further supporting the field-driven ionic displacement and gradual domain ordering in CBPS. Long-term synaptic plasticity was demonstrated by applying 50 potentiation pulses (+2.5 V, 10 ms) followed by 50 depression pulses (−1.2 V, 10 ms). As shown in Fig. 2f, the device conductance increases during potentiation and decreases during depression, with each cycle yielding reproducible and reversible behavior over ten iterations. This bidirectional plasticity closely mimics the dynamic modulation of synaptic strength in biological systems, underscoring the viability of CBPS memristors in implementing both short-term and long-term synaptic functions for neuromorphic computing architectures. In addition, noise robustness was confirmed by time-series and power spectral density (PSD) analyses, which showed stationary I(t) traces and 1/f α (α≈1) spectra without random telegraph noise features (Supplementary Fig. 14). Importantly, these synaptic plasticity characteristics were consistently observed across devices from different fabrication batches (Supplementary Figs. 15–17), confirming the reproducibility and robustness of the CBPS.

Voltage-dependent characteristics of long-term synaptic plasticity in CBPS-based memristors were investigated through a designed voltage-modulated stimulation protocol. As shown in Fig. 3a, each modulation cycle consisted of 10 consecutive pulses with linearly increasing amplitudes (1.2 V to 2.6 V) to emulate long-term potentiation (LTP), followed by a sequence of decreasing amplitudes (2.6 V to 1.2 V) to induce long-term depression (LTD), under the testing conditions summarized in Supplementary Fig. 18. This cycle was repeated 10 times, achieving stable bidirectional synaptic weight modulation purely by tuning the pulse amplitude, without altering pulse width or number. In addition to voltage-driven long-term plasticity, CBPS devices also emulate STDP, a fundamental rule governing timing-sensitive learning in biological synapses. Biologically, STDP modifies synaptic weight based on the time interval (Δt) between pre- and post-synaptic spikes: LTP occurs when the pre-spike precedes the post-spike (Δt > 0), while LTD is induced when the order is reversed (Δt < 0). A paired-pulse scheme was implemented using a single electrode, with a +3 V, 20 ms pulse representing the pre-spike and a −3 V, 20 ms pulse for the post-spike. Δt was varied from –200 ms to +200 ms. As shown in Fig. 3b, the resulting ΔG-Δt curve exhibits an asymmetric STDP window: potentiation in the positive Δt region and depression in the negative Δt region, consistent with biological behavior. To emulate triplet-STDP behavior observed in biological neurons, the conventional paired-pulse protocol was extended to a temporally controlled triplet-pulse scheme, as illustrated in Fig. 3c. Six pulse sequences composed of three voltage pulses (+3 V or –3 V, 20 ms each) were designed: Post-Pre-Pre, Pre-Post-Pre, Pre-Pre-Post, Pre-Post-Post, Post-Pre-Post, and Post-Post-Pre. Two-time intervals (Δt₁ and Δt₂) between adjacent spikes were defined, and the conductance change ΔG was mapped accordingly. Figure 3d, e display 2D heatmaps for representative patterns (Post-Pre-Post and Pre-Post-Pre), showing nonlinear dependence of synaptic weight on timing parameters, indicative of competitive and synergistic interactions between LTP and LTD processes. The mirrored symmetry between the two patterns highlights the system’s sensitivity to spike order. These behaviors originate from the internal polarization dynamics in CBPS: same-polarity pulses enhance Cu⁺ displacement and dipole alignment, while opposite or irregular sequences disturb the established polarization. BCM-type plasticity was further evaluated by applying identical stimulation parameters (+3 V, 20 ms) across varying pulse frequencies, starting from different initial conductance states (3.92, 7.0, and 16.1 nS). As shown in Fig. 3f, the ΔG-frequency curve exhibited a non-monotonic profile: depression at intermediate frequencies (~10-20 Hz) and potentiation at higher frequencies (>20 Hz). Importantly, the threshold frequency for the LTD-to-LTP transition decreased with increasing initial conductance, confirming a dynamic, activity-dependent modulation threshold. This sliding-threshold effect is in line with the core principle of the BCM rule, wherein synaptic modification thresholds adapt according to neuronal activity history. In addition, under fixed pulse parameters (+3 V, 20 ms; read voltage 0.5 V), the device’s response to different pulse frequencies was investigated (Fig. 3g). Four consecutive stimulation stages were applied sequentially: 25 Hz → 6.25 Hz → 1.47 Hz → 6.25 Hz. During the high-frequency stimulation (25 Hz), the device exhibited a significant conductance increase; as the frequency decreased to 6.25 Hz and 1.47 Hz, the conductance gradually decreased and stabilized; when the frequency was restored to 6.25 Hz, the conductance rose again. We also characterized the retention of ΔG after stimulation at different frequencies in the pre-post-pre mode, and the conductance of the device didn’t exhibit an obvious decrease over a period of 1000 s. (Supplementary Fig. 19). This frequency-dependent plasticity with history dependence reveals a sliding threshold mechanism, where synaptic potentiation or depression depends not only on the current frequency but also on the prior stimulation history, fully reflecting the key features of the BCM learning rule. A comparative analysis further confirms that the device exhibits biologically plausible time scales and plasticity rules (Table S1), and the benchmarking results highlight its notable advantages over existing 2D ferroelectric/antiferroelectric memristors (Table S2).

To emulate the biological functionalities of nociceptors, which are specialized sensory neurons responsible for detecting harmful mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli, we systematically investigated the pain-perception-mimicking behavior of memristive devices based on the CBPS relaxor AFE material. These nociceptive functionalities include not only threshold-triggered responses to intense stimuli, but also dynamic behaviors such as sensitization under repeated stimulation and desensitization after stimulus withdrawal. Figure 4a schematically illustrates the biological pain-perception pathway, where harmful stimuli are detected by peripheral sensory terminals (e.g., mechanoreceptors or thermoreceptors), transmitted through dorsal root ganglia to the spinal cord, and ultimately perceived in the cerebral cortex, triggering protective responses32,58,59. To mimic this process, we applied periodic voltage pulses with increasing amplitudes to the CBPS device and monitored the current response (Fig. 4b). At low input voltages, the device remained in a low-conductance state, reflecting an inert or adaptive phase. However, once the voltage surpassed a certain threshold, a sharp increase in current was observed. A threshold current of 2 μA was defined as the reference pain threshold, analogous to the excitability threshold of biological nociceptors. Below this value, the device remained quiescent; once exceeded, the response was regarded as a pain triggering event. This demonstrates the CBPS device’s ability to detect harmful stimuli with high sensitivity, emulating biological nociceptive behavior. To investigate sensitization, a phenomenon where previous strong stimuli enhance subsequent response, we applied pairs of pulses to the device. In each pair, the first pulse had increasing amplitudes ranging from 2.0 to 3.2 V, while the second pulse maintained a constant amplitude. As shown in Fig. 4c, the current response to the second (unchanged) pulse increased significantly with higher amplitudes of the first pulse, indicating a memory effect. This mimics pain sensitization, where a strong prior input heightens the system’s sensitivity to subsequent stimuli. A Pain Sensitization Index32,60 (PSI) was defined to quantify this behavior:

Sensitization Index = I 2nd / I 0 × 100% (1)

Here, I 2nd is the current induced by the second (detection) pulse, and I 0 is the reference current. As shown in Fig. 4e, PSI increases monotonically with the amplitude of the first pulse, validating the accumulation-driven sensitization in CBPS devices.

We further examined the pain desensitization behavior by applying a fixed high-amplitude sensitizing pulse (+3 V) followed by a constant lower-amplitude detection pulse (+2 V) with variable inter-pulse delay times Δt (20 ms to 320 ms). As illustrated in Fig. 4d, the response to the detection pulse gradually weakened as Δt increased. A Pain Desensitization Index (PDI) was defined as:

Desensitization Index = I 2nd / I 0 × 100% (2)

As shown in Fig. 4f, the pain desensitization index (PDI) decays exponentially with increasing Δt, indicating that prolonged intervals reduce excitability—analogous to the habituation behavior in biological nociceptors. In short intervals, the sensitizing pulse leaves the device in a highly excitable state, while longer delays allow relaxation, reducing the subsequent response. This emulates the biological desensitization process, where the nervous system becomes less responsive to repeated stimulation over time. Furthermore, Fig. 4g illustrates the effect of continuous stimulation on device behavior: under a prolonged train of identical electrical pulses, the output current gradually increases and eventually saturates, indicating an accumulation effect that mimics chronic pain sensitization observed in biological systems. This long-term potentiation of nociceptive response reflects the device’s ability to retain stimulus history and emulate persistent excitability. In summary, the CBPS memristive device not only demonstrates threshold-triggered responses to high-intensity stimuli but also reproduces dynamic sensitization, desensitization, and chronic excitation behavior. These features suggest its strong potential as a building block for artificial nociceptors in intelligent neuromorphic perception systems with reflexive and memory-like capabilities.

In neuromorphic computing systems, directly embedding memristive devices into deep neural network architectures presents a promising pathway toward efficient and compact intelligent information processing. Particularly for vision tasks such as image recognition, the high-density conductance states and synaptic plasticity of memristors can enable hardware-level integration of weight storage and forward inference, effectively reducing power consumption and latency61,62. To evaluate the practical applicability of the developed CBPS-based memristors in such neuromorphic architectures, a CNN model was implemented for face recognition tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 5a, the network comprises three convolution–pooling layers with kernel sizes of 32, 64, and 128, respectively, and 3 × 3 pooling operations. This is followed by two fully connected layers, and classification is performed via a Sigmoid activation function. The Olivetti Faces dataset, originally provided by AT&T Laboratories Cambridge, was used for this task, which consists of 400 grayscale images (64 × 64 pixels) of 40 individuals, each with 10 face images. The first 8 images per person were used for training (320 samples), and the remaining 2 for testing (80 samples). Figure 5b presents the recognition accuracy curves for both the CBPS-mapped network and an ideal digital model over training epochs. Both models converge within ~100 iterations, achieving final test accuracies of 91.3% (CBPS) and 93.7% (ideal), with only a 2.4% performance gap. This result demonstrates that the discrete and limited conductance states of CBPS memristors still support effective weight mapping in CNNs, and that their physical tunability is well aligned with neural network learning rules. Correspondingly, the loss convergence curves in Fig. 5c show that the CBPS-mapped network maintains a consistent and smooth error reduction trajectory, closely matching that of the ideal model, further confirming the memristor’s stability and dynamic response during training. To examine classification fidelity in greater detail, confusion matrices of the two models were compared. As shown in Fig. 5d, the ideal model exhibits a clear diagonal-dominant matrix, indicating highly accurate identification across all 40 facial classes. The CBPS-based model in Fig. 5e also presents a diagonal-dominated pattern, confirming its overall effective recognition capability. Minor off-diagonal misclassifications were observed in classes with visually similar features, likely due to the limited number of distinct conductance states or non-ideal tuning precision in the CBPS devices. The conductance update characteristics, statistical analyses of conductance variation (ΔG) under potentiation and depression processes were performed. As shown in Fig. 5f, potentiation-induced ΔG values are relatively stable in the low-conductance regime, whereas saturation and larger fluctuations occur at higher conductance states. In contrast, the depression pathway shown in Fig. 5g exhibits more linear and uniform ΔG distribution, suggesting improved consistency and stability during weight weakening. This asymmetric behavior indicates that CBPS memristors are particularly well suited for precise weight suppression, an essential property for efficient synaptic weight adjustment during network training. To further extend its neuromorphic computing applications, we conducted CNN simulations based on the MNIST handwritten digit recognition task. The results show that the CBPS-CNN network exhibits stable and superior classification performance in this task (Supplementary Fig. 20). Together, these results validate the integration potential of CBPS-based memristors in CNN architectures for neuromorphic computing, achieving robust pattern recognition performance with device-level conductance mapping and biologically plausible learning dynamics.

## Methods

Synthesis of CBPS crystals
High quality quaternary CBPS single crystals were synthesized via high Chemical Vapor Transport, CVT. Stoichiometric amounts of high-purity (all 99.99%) Cu, Bi, P, and Se were sealed in an evacuated 20 cm quartz ampule at 10⁻⁶ Torr and heated in a furnace. From ambient conditions, the temperature was increased to 870 °C within 48 h and held for ≈ 7 days. After heating, the furnace was allowed to cool to room temperature, upon which high-quality quaternary CBPS single crystals were obtained.

Characterization of CBPS
The crystal structure of quaternary CBPS was characterized using micro-XRD (Bruker D8 Discover). The elemental distribution of quaternary CBPS was characterized using a Quanta 400. The Raman spectra were performed by the WITec alpha300 Raman system with an excitation laser of 532 nm. The PFM measurements were performed using the Asylum Research MFP-3D and Cypher.

Device fabrication
The vertically structured sandwich devices were fabricated as follows: First, bottom electrodes consisting of Cr/Au (5 nm/45 nm) were patterned on a Si substrate with a 285 nm SiO₂ insulating layer using electron-beam lithography (DZS500) and deposited by thermal evaporation (DM400). Next, atomically thin CBPS flakes were mechanically exfoliated from bulk crystals and transferred onto the pre-patterned electrodes via a dry transfer method assisted by polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Pattering of CBPS was subsequently performed using reactive ion etching (RIE) (SHL 100u-RIE, Beijing SHL Semi. Equipment Co., Ltd.) to define the device area. Finally, top Cr/Au (5 nm/45 nm) electrodes were defined using a second electron-beam lithography step (DZS500) followed by thermal evaporation (DM400), completing the vertical device structure.

Device measurement
Measurements were performed under ambient vacuum conditions using a Keithley 4200A-SCS and Keithley 2636B semiconductor parameter analyzer in a probe station (CRX-6.5, LakeShore). The ferroelectric measurement was performed by ferroelectric analyzer (Huace FE-2000 Analyzer) in a probe station (CRX-6.5, LakeShore).

demonstrated that the polarization behavior in CBPS could be primarily governed by field-

obtained from P-E measurements and the reversible domain contrast observed via PFM,
confirming the relaxor antiferroelectric nature of CBPS. Building on this intrinsic Cu⁺ ion
displacement–polarization mechanism, we constructed CBPS-based memristor devices capable
of emulating multiple neuromorphic functions. Notably, both the BCM learning rule and
nociceptor-like behaviors are realized through continuous and programmable conductance
modulation under specific voltage pulse parameters. These functions share the same underlying
origin—Cu⁺ ion displacement–driven polarization switching—which enables dynamic weight
adaptation and threshold sliding analogous to biological synapses without the need for complex
peripheral circuits. Therefore, the synaptic plasticity features such as potentiation/depression,
sliding-threshold learning, and dynamic current responses are not independent effects, but
rather emergent behaviors arising from the intrinsic polarization dynamics induced by Cu⁺ ion
displacement.

Comment 6:
What experimental data confirms that the nociceptor behavior and BCM learning are
governed by Cu⁺ displacement and not generic ionic drift or Joule heating?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical question. The AFE behavior of CBPS
provides the physical foundation for realizing both the BCM learning rule and nociceptor-like
functions. Under an external electric field, CBPS exhibits clear and reversible polarization
switching, which is intrinsically governed by the displacement of Cu⁺ ions. This mechanism
enables the devices to achieve high controllability, multi-stable states, and gradual conductance
modulation—key attributes essential for mimicking biological synaptic functionalities.
Moreover, theoretical studies 1,2 have explicitly demonstrated that the AFE polarization
transition in CBPS is driven by cooperative Cu⁺ ion displacement. This displacement is closely
related to the unstable coordination of Cu⁺ ions in the quasi-octahedral voids and is
strongly influenced by the second-order Jahn–Teller (SOJT) effect, leading to local non-
centrosymmetric distortion and triggering polarization reversal. It is precisely this SOJT-
driven Cu⁺ ion displacement mechanism that gives CBPS its characteristic relaxor
antiferroelectric properties.
In our work, we further validate this mechanism through the following experimental
observations:
Polarization switching and reversible PFM response confirm field-controllable
polarization: We observed typical double hysteresis P-E loops, and PFM measurements
revealed reversible phase-contrast changes under bipolar voltage sweeps. These results confirm
the reversible nature of polarization in CBPS, with good repeatability and directionality,
effectively ruling out stochastic ionic drift or Joule-heating–driven mechanisms.
Consistent LTP/LTD responses support synaptic plasticity capability: As shown in
Figure 2f, the devices exhibit highly consistent conductance modulation under repeated
LTP and LTD pulse trains, further ruling out stochastic ionic drift or Joule-heating–
driven mechanisms. Such gradual and bidirectional conductance evolution is difficult to
achieve through generic ionic drift or unstable thermal effects, and is more plausibly attributed
to the intrinsic polarization control enabled by Cu⁺ ion displacement.
In summary, we believe that the observed neuromorphic functionalities are not governed
by generic electrochemical effects or Joule heating, but are intrinsically rooted in the
polarization-regulating mechanism driven by Cu⁺ ion displacement under the influence of the
SOJT effect in the CBPS lattice.

networks, the synaptic weights are represented by the conductance states of the device array.
Conductance drift after training can alter the stored weight matrix, which may significantly

nonlinearity—the nonlinear dependence of conductance changes on initial conductance—can
negatively impact training, as it leads to inconsistent update magnitudes across different weight
ranges, introducing weight update errors. Saturation effects at the conductance extremes further
exacerbate this issue by limiting the available dynamic range for weight tuning. Therefore, both
nonlinearity and drift must be carefully considered in device modeling and compensated for via
training algorithms or circuit-level calibration to ensure stable learning and inference
performance.

What physical or chemical signatures differentiate synaptic modulation from ionic drift
or dielectric breakdown in these devices?
Reply: We thank the reviewer for raising this critical question. In our study, the synaptic
plasticity behaviors observed in CBPS-based devices—including LTP/LTD and BCM
learning—originate from Cu⁺ ion-driven polarization modulation rather than generic ionic drift
or dielectric breakdown. This distinction is supported by multiple experimental observations:
1.cycling stability: The I-V characteristics remain smooth and stable across repeated
measurements, with no evidence of abrupt current jumps or breakdown events, thereby
excluding breakdown-dominated mechanisms.
2.Gradual and repeatable conductance modulation: The device exhibits continuous
and reproducible conductance evolution under repeated stimulation pulses. The progressive
nature of the LTP/LTD curves reflects a controlled and reversible modulation process, which is
inconsistent with random, irreversible conductive filament formation typically seen in ionic
drift or breakdown phenomena.
3.PFM and P-E evidence for polarization-controlled behavior: We measured
characteristic double-loop P-E hysteresis curves and observed reversible phase contrast
changes in PFM under applied bias. These results directly link the conductance modulation to
reversible polarization states, reinforcing that the underlying mechanism is governed by field-
induced Cu⁺ ion displacement within the CBPS lattice.
Taken together, these findings strongly indicate that the neuromorphic behaviors in our
devices are not driven by conventional ionic drift or Joule heating, but rather by the intrinsic
polarization modulation mechanism driven by Cu⁺ ion displacement. This mechanism provides
implementing reliable and bioinspired synaptic functionalities in hardware.
Comment 17:
Can the authors demonstrate scalable, CMOS-compatible fabrication beyond manual
exfoliation and lithography?

work is to elucidate the intrinsic polarization dynamics and neuromorphic functionalities of
CBPS. To ensure material integrity and fabrication precision, we employed mechanical
exfoliation and EBL to prepare high-quality prototype devices at the proof-of-concept stage.
We fully agree with the reviewer that scalable and CMOS-compatible fabrication processes are
crucial for future device integration. It is worth emphasizing that CBPS shares structural
similarity with other van der Waals layered chalcogenides (e.g., transition metal
dichalcogenides), many of which have already been successfully synthesized on a large scale
via chemical vapor deposition (CVD) or molecular beam epitaxy (MBE). This provides a
feasible route toward wafer-scale growth of CBPS.
However, owing to the complex synthetic pathways of quaternary polar vdW materials
and the multitude of physicochemical parameters, achieving wafer-scale CBPS samples
represents a worldwide challenge. Addressing this issue calls for collective efforts from the
global materials research community and is beyond the scope of the present work. We hope that
the reviewer can understand these issues and challenges.

## Paper

## Abstract

Antiferroelectric two-dimensional materials, with their unique physical mechanisms, exhibit tunable polarization dynamics and layered structural characteristics, enabling the synergistic implementation of synaptic plasticity, sensory-mimetic functionality, and in-memory computing within a unified device architecture. These capabilities meet the growing polymorphic requirements of neuromorphic systems and position such materials as strong candidates for next-generation neuromorphic computing platforms. Among them, CuBiP₂Se₆ stands out among 2D antiferroelectric materials due to its intrinsic antiferroelectric properties, featuring a stable interlayer antiparallel Cu⁺ dipole configuration. This structure, combined with its relaxor-like behavior, enables a reversible transition between antiferroelectric and ferroelectric states under an applied electric field, along with gradual polarization tuning. This transition mechanism enables continuously tunable conductance states, providing essential physical support for the gradual modulation of synaptic weights and the hardware implementation of complex neural functions, making it particularly suited for high-precision emulation of multilevel synaptic plasticity in neuromorphic applications. In this work, memristor based on two-dimensional antiferroelectric CuBiP₂Se₆ exhibit stable multilevel conductance states, high endurance, and excellent device uniformity, thus supporting diverse neurosynaptic functions and advanced learning rules. These attributes highlight the immense potential of antiferroelectric 2D materials as a foundation for compact, energy-efficient, and highly integrated neuromorphic hardware.

---

## Introduction

The surging demand for energy-efficient, multifunctional computing power has revealed the limitations of traditional von Neumann architectures, notably serial processing and escalating power dissipation1–6. As a result, neuromorphic computing, which is modeled on the parallel and low-information processing of the brain, has come to the forefront7,8. Next-generation neuromorphic systems require hardware capable of emulating complex biological learning rules and supporting a broad spectrum of synaptic functions9–14. While memristors have advanced in-memory and compute-in-memory architectures by leveraging their analog and nonvolatile resistive switching, most current devices- as illustrated in Fig. 1a are limited to first-order synaptic dynamics, such as short-term plasticity (STP) and basic spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP)15–18. Although STDP circuits excel at certain tasks, their reinforcement-based nature restricts synaptic stability and adaptability, making them inadequate for capturing the richer temporal and rate-based synaptic modulation observed in biological systems19.

To address these challenges, materials and device platforms must go beyond simple Hebbian learning, enabling history-dependent, nonlinear, and homeostatic plasticity like BCM (Bienenstock-Cooper-Munro) learning20–33. Among them, the BCM rule17,34 represents a rate-based synaptic plasticity model that extends the classical Hebbian paradigm by introducing the average postsynaptic firing rate as a regulatory factor, thereby enabling synaptic weight updates to reflect the historical activity of the neuron (Fig. 1b). Theoretically, the time-dependent dynamic processes inherent in physical mechanisms such as ion migration and trap-state modulation offer promising avenues for implementing history-dependent and nonlinearly evolving weight updates required by the BCM rule24–26,30. However, the practical realization of BCM-compatible behavior and the required multifunctional synaptic modulation at the device level still faces considerable challenges, such as unstable conductive pathways, poor performance uniformity, limited reproducibility, and insufficient endurance. These issues are primarily attributed to the immaturity of material systems, the high complexity of multifunctional integration, and the challenges associated with device fabrication processes.

Compared with conventional ferroelectric (FE) systems, antiferroelectric (AFE) materials—with their near-zero remanent polarization and antiparallel dipole configurations—can achieve analog, continuously tunable conductance modulation, making them ideal candidates for energy-efficient neuromorphic devices35–39. Their unique polarization-switching mechanism further endows them with higher breakdown fields36,40, faster polarization switching speeds41,42, lower energy dissipation36,43, and excellent fatigue resistance44,45. In particular, relaxor-type AFE materials exhibit gradual polarization responses under external electric fields and slowly relax back once the field is removed46,47. Such dynamical characteristics more closely resemble the time-dependent and history-sensitive behaviors of biological synapses, rendering them especially suitable for hardware implementation of sliding-threshold regulation in BCM-type plasticity.

To the best of our knowledge, the van der Waals layered compound CuBiP₂Se₆ (CBPS) is the first 2D AFE semiconductor and have outstanding properties: it possesses intrinsic antiferroelectric order with antiparallel dipoles, enabling nonlinear, history-dependent, and analog conductance modulation. Furthermore, its dangling-bond-free surfaces and atomically thin geometry ensure excellent interfacial quality, scalability, and compatibility with silicon-based CMOS technologies48–52, distinguishing CBPS as a promising platform for mimicking complex synaptic functionalities in neuromorphic applications.

In this work, we report a vertical memristor array based on 2D relaxor AFE CBPS. The devices exhibit robust multilevel conductance modulation, stable bipolar switching (sustaining over 1000 cycles), and an overall yield exceeding 90%, reflecting high process reproducibility. Neuromorphic functionalities include paired-pulse facilitation, long-term potentiation/depression, and, through triplet-STDP pulse protocols, device-level manifestation of frequency-dependent weight updates and a sliding plasticity threshold effectively mimics key aspects of BCM learning, enabling advanced forms of synaptic plasticity crucial for adaptive information processing. In addition, the devices demonstrate electrically driven nociceptor-like responses, responding sharply to suprathreshold inputs; this is analogous to how biological systems prioritize the rapid transmission of critical or potentially harmful sensory information. The integration of both BCM-type learning and nociceptive response in a single device reflects the polymorphic nature required for robust neuromorphic computing. Leveraging these dynamic synaptic features, device characteristics were mapped into an artificial neural network for facial recognition. The advanced synaptic plasticity empowered by BCM learning, together with the adaptive sensitivity derived from nociceptor-like response, jointly contribute to more effective feature extraction and information discrimination within the neural network. As a result, the system achieves a classification accuracy exceeding 90%, demonstrating not only excellent trainability but also the practical value of integrating diverse synaptic behaviors within neuromorphic hardware for next-generation artificial intelligence applications. This work establishes antiferroelectric 2D materials—specifically CBPS—as a powerful platform for polymorphic neuromorphic devices, combining fine-tuned and reliable synaptic emulation with CMOS compatibility and integration potential. These advances mark a significant step toward energy-efficient, highly adaptive brain-inspired hardware that can tackle the increasingly complex demands of future computing systems.

---

## Results

The crystal structure of CBPS is illustrated in Fig. 1c (top view) and Fig. 1e (side view). To verify the chemical composition and structural integrity of the synthesized CBPS single crystals, comprehensive characterizations were conducted, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 1 Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) revealed a molar ratio of Cu, Bi, P, and Se close to 1:1:2:6, in good agreement with the theoretical stoichiometry of CBPS, confirming successful synthesis of the target compound. Elemental mapping further demonstrated uniform spatial distribution of the constituent elements across the nanosheet, without apparent aggregation or depletion, indicating excellent compositional homogeneity. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) images, as shown in Fig. 1d, reveal well-aligned lattice fringes with no observable structural defects, indicating high crystal quality and a layered structure. In addition, the corresponding selected area electron diffraction (SAED) pattern displays sharp and well-defined diffraction spots with hexagonal symmetry, further confirming the single-crystalline nature of the CBPS flakes (Supplementary Fig. 2). In addition, the X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern displayed in Supplementary Fig. 2 shows sharp and well-defined diffraction peaks that match well with the standard CBPS pattern, further confirming the phase purity and structural consistency of the material. The Raman spectrum of CBPS, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 3, exhibits several characteristic peaks at 111.7, 135.3, 207.5, 431.9, and 465.9 cm⁻¹. According to previous reports47,53–55, the low-frequency peaks at 111.7 and 135.3 cm⁻¹ are associated with lattice vibrations involving Bi-Se and Cu-Se bonds, while the dominant peak at 207.5 cm⁻¹ is attributed to the symmetric stretching vibration of the [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ unit. The higher-frequency peaks at 431.9 and 465.9 cm⁻¹ correspond to the P-Se bond stretching vibrations within the [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ group. Based on symmetry considerations, the peaks labeled in red represent out-of-plane modes, whereas those in blue correspond to in-plane modes. At room temperature, CBPS exhibits distinct AFE behavior. First-principles calculations by Reimers et al.46,47 suggest that CBPS consists of layered [P₂Se₆]⁴⁻ anionic frameworks interleaved with Cu⁺ and Bi³⁺ cations. Cu⁺ ions typically occupy octahedral sites, but due to their small ionic radius and weak coordination bonding, they tend to shift either vertically or laterally53 (Supplementary Fig. 4). These displacements modulate the local coordination environment, thereby tuning the polarization state and enabling electric-field-induced transitions between FE and AFE phases. When Cu⁺ ions displace vertically, local dipoles are formed. If adjacent layers exhibit opposite displacement directions, the resulting interlayer dipoles cancel out, leading to near-zero net polarization—a hallmark of AFE order.

Under a sufficiently strong electric field, the Cu⁺ ions align in the same direction, generating net polarization and inducing a transition from AFE to FE state, as illustrated in the schematic in Fig. 1e. This transition is typically accompanied by pronounced polarization responses. The AFE nature of CBPS was further validated by polarization-electric field (P-E) hysteresis measurements. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 5, the optical microscopy image and atomic force microscopy (AFM) scan reveal a ~20 nm-thick CBPS flake uniformly bridging the crossbar electrodes, ensuring a stable interface for electrical characterization. As shown in Fig. 1f, the device exhibits a characteristic double-loop P-E profile under an applied electric field. Unlike classical AFE materials that undergo abrupt polarization switching, CBPS shows smooth and gradual P-E loops, indicating a relaxor response. This behavior is attributed to the progressive alignment of initially disordered polar nanoregions under the electric field, a signature of relaxor AFE materials56,57. Furthermore, typical relaxor antiferroelectric features were consistently observed across a wide temperature range (210−330 K) and in devices with different thicknesses, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 6-7. This process was further corroborated by piezoresponse force microscopy (PFM) analysis. As shown in Fig. 1g, the PFM phase signal becomes increasingly pronounced upon continuous electrical stimulation, indicating electric-field-induced domain reorientation. In parallel, the corresponding PFM amplitude mapping shows a significant enhancement in signal intensity, reflecting a progressive increase in local piezoelectric response. These observations are consistent with the accumulation of aligned dipoles and confirm the presence of electric-field-driven domain evolution in CBPS. The characterization results confirm that the synthesized CBPS crystals exhibit a well-ordered layered structure, high crystallinity, and uniform composition. Their relaxor AFE behavior with smooth, tunable polarization and reversible transitions provides a reliable basis for CBPS-based memristor design and neuromorphic applications.

A vertical 5 × 5 memristor array was fabricated using the two-dimensional relaxor antiferroelectric material CBPS as the active layer, as schematically illustrated in Fig. 2a, with the optical image shown in Supplementary Fig. 8. Electrical measurements reveal that the device exhibits clear bipolar resistive switching under ±1.5 V voltage sweeps (Fig. 2b), which can be attributed to field-driven vertical Cu⁺ ion displacement and the associated polarization modulation. A compliance current of 100 μA was applied during testing to avoid over-current damage, and the high-resistance state (HRS) and low-resistance state (LRS) values were consistently extracted at a reading voltage of 0.5 V. Under these conditions, the device maintains a high ON/OFF conductance ratio (>10²) over 1000 consecutive switching cycles without performance degradation, demonstrating excellent endurance. The statistical distribution of HRS and LRS values over 1000 cycles, presented in Supplementary Fig. 9, together with the consecutive I–V switching characteristics of the CBPS-based memristor that remain stable even after 100 days (Supplementary Fig. 10) further confirms the stability and reproducibility of the resistive switching behavior. These results highlight that the layered crystal structure and antipolar configuration of CBPS enable robust and reversible switching characteristics. Additionally, the fabricated 5 × 5 array exhibited a device yield of 92% (23 out of 25 devices), which successfully demonstrated stable neuromorphic behaviors, including nonlinear current–voltage characteristics and reliable multi-pulse conductance responses (Supplementary Fig. 11-12), confirming the device’s reliability and compatibility with large-scale integration. Short-term synaptic plasticity characteristics were evaluated by applying paired voltage pulses (3 V, 20 ms) with varying inter-pulse intervals (Δt = 20–500 ms). As depicted in Fig. 2c, the second excitatory postsynaptic current (A₂) consistently exceeds the first (A₁), and the PPF index (A₂/A₁ × 100%) decays exponentially with increasing interval, closely emulating neurotransmitter residual effects observed in biological synapses.

The synaptic weight modulation was further investigated by tuning the pulse amplitude, number, and width. When increasing the write voltage from 3 V to 8 V under otherwise identical conditions (20 pulses, 20 ms interval), the device exhibits a stepwise increase in conductance under a non-destructive read voltage of 0.5 V (Fig. 2d). The inset highlights a cumulative increase in current with stronger electric fields, indicating enhanced Cu⁺ displacement and dipole alignment. Under fixed pulse conditions (3 V, 20 ms), the conductance increases progressively with pulse number (10, 20, 50) and saturates at higher levels (Fig. 2e), revealing a characteristic accumulation effect. Pulse width also plays a significant role: extending the duration from 1 ms to 40 ms results in notably higher conductance (Supplementary Fig. 13), further supporting the field-driven ionic displacement and gradual domain ordering in CBPS. Long-term synaptic plasticity was demonstrated by applying 50 potentiation pulses (+2.5 V, 10 ms) followed by 50 depression pulses (−1.2 V, 10 ms). As shown in Fig. 2f, the device conductance increases during potentiation and decreases during depression, with each cycle yielding reproducible and reversible behavior over ten iterations. This bidirectional plasticity closely mimics the dynamic modulation of synaptic strength in biological systems, underscoring the viability of CBPS memristors in implementing both short-term and long-term synaptic functions for neuromorphic computing architectures. In addition, noise robustness was confirmed by time-series and power spectral density (PSD) analyses, which showed stationary I(t) traces and 1/f α (α≈1) spectra without random telegraph noise features (Supplementary Fig. 14). Importantly, these synaptic plasticity characteristics were consistently observed across devices from different fabrication batches (Supplementary Figs. 15–17), confirming the reproducibility and robustness of the CBPS.

Voltage-dependent characteristics of long-term synaptic plasticity in CBPS-based memristors were investigated through a designed voltage-modulated stimulation protocol. As shown in Fig. 3a, each modulation cycle consisted of 10 consecutive pulses with linearly increasing amplitudes (1.2 V to 2.6 V) to emulate long-term potentiation (LTP), followed by a sequence of decreasing amplitudes (2.6 V to 1.2 V) to induce long-term depression (LTD), under the testing conditions summarized in Supplementary Fig. 18. This cycle was repeated 10 times, achieving stable bidirectional synaptic weight modulation purely by tuning the pulse amplitude, without altering pulse width or number. In addition to voltage-driven long-term plasticity, CBPS devices also emulate STDP, a fundamental rule governing timing-sensitive learning in biological synapses. Biologically, STDP modifies synaptic weight based on the time interval (Δt) between pre- and post-synaptic spikes: LTP occurs when the pre-spike precedes the post-spike (Δt > 0), while LTD is induced when the order is reversed (Δt < 0). A paired-pulse scheme was implemented using a single electrode, with a +3 V, 20 ms pulse representing the pre-spike and a −3 V, 20 ms pulse for the post-spike. Δt was varied from –200 ms to +200 ms. As shown in Fig. 3b, the resulting ΔG-Δt curve exhibits an asymmetric STDP window: potentiation in the positive Δt region and depression in the negative Δt region, consistent with biological behavior. To emulate triplet-STDP behavior observed in biological neurons, the conventional paired-pulse protocol was extended to a temporally controlled triplet-pulse scheme, as illustrated in Fig. 3c. Six pulse sequences composed of three voltage pulses (+3 V or –3 V, 20 ms each) were designed: Post-Pre-Pre, Pre-Post-Pre, Pre-Pre-Post, Pre-Post-Post, Post-Pre-Post, and Post-Post-Pre. Two-time intervals (Δt₁ and Δt₂) between adjacent spikes were defined, and the conductance change ΔG was mapped accordingly. Figure 3d, e display 2D heatmaps for representative patterns (Post-Pre-Post and Pre-Post-Pre), showing nonlinear dependence of synaptic weight on timing parameters, indicative of competitive and synergistic interactions between LTP and LTD processes. The mirrored symmetry between the two patterns highlights the system’s sensitivity to spike order. These behaviors originate from the internal polarization dynamics in CBPS: same-polarity pulses enhance Cu⁺ displacement and dipole alignment, while opposite or irregular sequences disturb the established polarization. BCM-type plasticity was further evaluated by applying identical stimulation parameters (+3 V, 20 ms) across varying pulse frequencies, starting from different initial conductance states (3.92, 7.0, and 16.1 nS). As shown in Fig. 3f, the ΔG-frequency curve exhibited a non-monotonic profile: depression at intermediate frequencies (~10-20 Hz) and potentiation at higher frequencies (>20 Hz). Importantly, the threshold frequency for the LTD-to-LTP transition decreased with increasing initial conductance, confirming a dynamic, activity-dependent modulation threshold. This sliding-threshold effect is in line with the core principle of the BCM rule, wherein synaptic modification thresholds adapt according to neuronal activity history. In addition, under fixed pulse parameters (+3 V, 20 ms; read voltage 0.5 V), the device’s response to different pulse frequencies was investigated (Fig. 3g). Four consecutive stimulation stages were applied sequentially: 25 Hz → 6.25 Hz → 1.47 Hz → 6.25 Hz. During the high-frequency stimulation (25 Hz), the device exhibited a significant conductance increase; as the frequency decreased to 6.25 Hz and 1.47 Hz, the conductance gradually decreased and stabilized; when the frequency was restored to 6.25 Hz, the conductance rose again. We also characterized the retention of ΔG after stimulation at different frequencies in the pre-post-pre mode, and the conductance of the device didn’t exhibit an obvious decrease over a period of 1000 s. (Supplementary Fig. 19). This frequency-dependent plasticity with history dependence reveals a sliding threshold mechanism, where synaptic potentiation or depression depends not only on the current frequency but also on the prior stimulation history, fully reflecting the key features of the BCM learning rule. A comparative analysis further confirms that the device exhibits biologically plausible time scales and plasticity rules (Table S1), and the benchmarking results highlight its notable advantages over existing 2D ferroelectric/antiferroelectric memristors (Table S2).

To emulate the biological functionalities of nociceptors, which are specialized sensory neurons responsible for detecting harmful mechanical, thermal, or chemical stimuli, we systematically investigated the pain-perception-mimicking behavior of memristive devices based on the CBPS relaxor AFE material. These nociceptive functionalities include not only threshold-triggered responses to intense stimuli, but also dynamic behaviors such as sensitization under repeated stimulation and desensitization after stimulus withdrawal. Figure 4a schematically illustrates the biological pain-perception pathway, where harmful stimuli are detected by peripheral sensory terminals (e.g., mechanoreceptors or thermoreceptors), transmitted through dorsal root ganglia to the spinal cord, and ultimately perceived in the cerebral cortex, triggering protective responses32,58,59. To mimic this process, we applied periodic voltage pulses with increasing amplitudes to the CBPS device and monitored the current response (Fig. 4b). At low input voltages, the device remained in a low-conductance state, reflecting an inert or adaptive phase. However, once the voltage surpassed a certain threshold, a sharp increase in current was observed. A threshold current of 2 μA was defined as the reference pain threshold, analogous to the excitability threshold of biological nociceptors. Below this value, the device remained quiescent; once exceeded, the response was regarded as a pain triggering event. This demonstrates the CBPS device’s ability to detect harmful stimuli with high sensitivity, emulating biological nociceptive behavior. To investigate sensitization, a phenomenon where previous strong stimuli enhance subsequent response, we applied pairs of pulses to the device. In each pair, the first pulse had increasing amplitudes ranging from 2.0 to 3.2 V, while the second pulse maintained a constant amplitude. As shown in Fig. 4c, the current response to the second (unchanged) pulse increased significantly with higher amplitudes of the first pulse, indicating a memory effect. This mimics pain sensitization, where a strong prior input heightens the system’s sensitivity to subsequent stimuli. A Pain Sensitization Index32,60 (PSI) was defined to quantify this behavior:

Sensitization Index = I 2nd / I 0 × 100% (1)

Here, I 2nd is the current induced by the second (detection) pulse, and I 0 is the reference current. As shown in Fig. 4e, PSI increases monotonically with the amplitude of the first pulse, validating the accumulation-driven sensitization in CBPS devices.

We further examined the pain desensitization behavior by applying a fixed high-amplitude sensitizing pulse (+3 V) followed by a constant lower-amplitude detection pulse (+2 V) with variable inter-pulse delay times Δt (20 ms to 320 ms). As illustrated in Fig. 4d, the response to the detection pulse gradually weakened as Δt increased. A Pain Desensitization Index (PDI) was defined as:

Desensitization Index = I 2nd / I 0 × 100% (2)

As shown in Fig. 4f, the pain desensitization index (PDI) decays exponentially with increasing Δt, indicating that prolonged intervals reduce excitability—analogous to the habituation behavior in biological nociceptors. In short intervals, the sensitizing pulse leaves the device in a highly excitable state, while longer delays allow relaxation, reducing the subsequent response. This emulates the biological desensitization process, where the nervous system becomes less responsive to repeated stimulation over time. Furthermore, Fig. 4g illustrates the effect of continuous stimulation on device behavior: under a prolonged train of identical electrical pulses, the output current gradually increases and eventually saturates, indicating an accumulation effect that mimics chronic pain sensitization observed in biological systems. This long-term potentiation of nociceptive response reflects the device’s ability to retain stimulus history and emulate persistent excitability. In summary, the CBPS memristive device not only demonstrates threshold-triggered responses to high-intensity stimuli but also reproduces dynamic sensitization, desensitization, and chronic excitation behavior. These features suggest its strong potential as a building block for artificial nociceptors in intelligent neuromorphic perception systems with reflexive and memory-like capabilities.

In neuromorphic computing systems, directly embedding memristive devices into deep neural network architectures presents a promising pathway toward efficient and compact intelligent information processing. Particularly for vision tasks such as image recognition, the high-density conductance states and synaptic plasticity of memristors can enable hardware-level integration of weight storage and forward inference, effectively reducing power consumption and latency61,62. To evaluate the practical applicability of the developed CBPS-based memristors in such neuromorphic architectures, a CNN model was implemented for face recognition tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 5a, the network comprises three convolution–pooling layers with kernel sizes of 32, 64, and 128, respectively, and 3 × 3 pooling operations. This is followed by two fully connected layers, and classification is performed via a Sigmoid activation function. The Olivetti Faces dataset, originally provided by AT&T Laboratories Cambridge, was used for this task, which consists of 400 grayscale images (64 × 64 pixels) of 40 individuals, each with 10 face images. The first 8 images per person were used for training (320 samples), and the remaining 2 for testing (80 samples). Figure 5b presents the recognition accuracy curves for both the CBPS-mapped network and an ideal digital model over training epochs. Both models converge within ~100 iterations, achieving final test accuracies of 91.3% (CBPS) and 93.7% (ideal), with only a 2.4% performance gap. This result demonstrates that the discrete and limited conductance states of CBPS memristors still support effective weight mapping in CNNs, and that their physical tunability is well aligned with neural network learning rules. Correspondingly, the loss convergence curves in Fig. 5c show that the CBPS-mapped network maintains a consistent and smooth error reduction trajectory, closely matching that of the ideal model, further confirming the memristor’s stability and dynamic response during training. To examine classification fidelity in greater detail, confusion matrices of the two models were compared. As shown in Fig. 5d, the ideal model exhibits a clear diagonal-dominant matrix, indicating highly accurate identification across all 40 facial classes. The CBPS-based model in Fig. 5e also presents a diagonal-dominated pattern, confirming its overall effective recognition capability. Minor off-diagonal misclassifications were observed in classes with visually similar features, likely due to the limited number of distinct conductance states or non-ideal tuning precision in the CBPS devices. The conductance update characteristics, statistical analyses of conductance variation (ΔG) under potentiation and depression processes were performed. As shown in Fig. 5f, potentiation-induced ΔG values are relatively stable in the low-conductance regime, whereas saturation and larger fluctuations occur at higher conductance states. In contrast, the depression pathway shown in Fig. 5g exhibits more linear and uniform ΔG distribution, suggesting improved consistency and stability during weight weakening. This asymmetric behavior indicates that CBPS memristors are particularly well suited for precise weight suppression, an essential property for efficient synaptic weight adjustment during network training. To further extend its neuromorphic computing applications, we conducted CNN simulations based on the MNIST handwritten digit recognition task. The results show that the CBPS-CNN network exhibits stable and superior classification performance in this task (Supplementary Fig. 20). Together, these results validate the integration potential of CBPS-based memristors in CNN architectures for neuromorphic computing, achieving robust pattern recognition performance with device-level conductance mapping and biologically plausible learning dynamics.

## Methods

Synthesis of CBPS crystals
High quality quaternary CBPS single crystals were synthesized via high Chemical Vapor Transport, CVT. Stoichiometric amounts of high-purity (all 99.99%) Cu, Bi, P, and Se were sealed in an evacuated 20 cm quartz ampule at 10⁻⁶ Torr and heated in a furnace. From ambient conditions, the temperature was increased to 870 °C within 48 h and held for ≈ 7 days. After heating, the furnace was allowed to cool to room temperature, upon which high-quality quaternary CBPS single crystals were obtained.

Characterization of CBPS
The crystal structure of quaternary CBPS was characterized using micro-XRD (Bruker D8 Discover). The elemental distribution of quaternary CBPS was characterized using a Quanta 400. The Raman spectra were performed by the WITec alpha300 Raman system with an excitation laser of 532 nm. The PFM measurements were performed using the Asylum Research MFP-3D and Cypher.

Device fabrication
The vertically structured sandwich devices were fabricated as follows: First, bottom electrodes consisting of Cr/Au (5 nm/45 nm) were patterned on a Si substrate with a 285 nm SiO₂ insulating layer using electron-beam lithography (DZS500) and deposited by thermal evaporation (DM400). Next, atomically thin CBPS flakes were mechanically exfoliated from bulk crystals and transferred onto the pre-patterned electrodes via a dry transfer method assisted by polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS). Pattering of CBPS was subsequently performed using reactive ion etching (RIE) (SHL 100u-RIE, Beijing SHL Semi. Equipment Co., Ltd.) to define the device area. Finally, top Cr/Au (5 nm/45 nm) electrodes were defined using a second electron-beam lithography step (DZS500) followed by thermal evaporation (DM400), completing the vertical device structure.

Device measurement
Measurements were performed under ambient vacuum conditions using a Keithley 4200A-SCS and Keithley 2636B semiconductor parameter analyzer in a probe station (CRX-6.5, LakeShore). The ferroelectric measurement was performed by ferroelectric analyzer (Huace FE-2000 Analyzer) in a probe station (CRX-6.5, LakeShore).

clarify that the CBPS nanoflakes used in this study were mechanically exfoliated from
bulk single crystals grown by the CVT (Chemical Vapor Transport) method. The single-
crystalline nature of the bulk CBPS has been verified by XRD and SAED analyses.
Therefore, the term “single crystal” in our manuscript refers to the source material,
while the device nanoflakes were obtained from this bulk single crystal by mechanical
exfoliation. This approach is widely used in 2D materials research1,2,3, and preserves
the intrinsic layered order and single-crystalline characteristics of the material.
Regarding nanoflake thickness screening, we systematically tested devices
fabricated from nanoflakes of different thicknesses (10 nm, 18 nm, 23 nm, 26 nm, and
32 nm) (Figure R15a-e), and all devices were subjected to 1000 consecutive I-V cycles.
The results show that devices with thicknesses in the range of 18-26 nm exhibited the
most stable and reproducible gradual I-V conductance modulation. Devices at the
thicknesses of 10 nm and 32 nm also displayed gradual modulation, but with narrower
stability windows. For the fabrication of the 5×5 device array, we selected a 22 nm
CBPS nanoflake, which lies within the optimal range. Importantly, this was a exfoliated
nano nanoflake with large size that was transferred onto the pre-patterned 5×5 electrode
array, ensuring that all 25 devices originated from the same nano nanoflake thickness.
This inherently guarantees uniformity in thickness, orientation, and crystal quality
across the array and avoids variations that may arise from different nano nanoflakes.
As for the fabrication process of the 5×5 array: (1) electron-beam lithography
(EBL) was first used to define the bottom electrode patterns, followed by Cr/Au
deposition via thermal evaporation; (2) a 22 nm CBPS nanoflake obtained by
mechanical exfoliation was then precisely transferred onto the pre-patterned electrode
region; (3) after the transfer of nano nanoflake, EBL and etching, were further employed
to define the active device regions, thereby providing physical isolation between
neighboring cells and ensuring that each device operated independently without
electrical crosstalk; (4) finally, EBL and metal deposition were used again to form the
top electrodes, completing the construction of the 5×5 array. This fabrication process
guarantees that all devices within the array share the same thickness, orientation, and
crystalline quality, while also ensuring reliable inter-device isolation and
reproducibility.

First, CBPS is a typical van der Waals layered material, in which adjacent layers are
bonded by weak van der Waals forces. This property allows high-quality thin nanoflakes to be
mechanically exfoliated from bulk single crystals while preserving their ordered layered
structure and crystalline integrity. Therefore, the term “single crystal” in our manuscript refers
to the bulk crystals grown by the CVT method, while the device nanoflakes were obtained from
this bulk single crystal by mechanical exfoliation, a widely adopted approach in 2D materials
research.
Second, during device fabrication, we conducted a rigorous screening of the nanoflake
thickness. These devices with different nanoflake thicknesses (10 nm, 18 nm, 23 nm, 26 nm,
and 32 nm) were systematically tested under 1000 consecutive I-V switching cycles. The results
indicate that devices with thicknesses in the range of 18–26 nm exhibit excellent stability and
highly reproducible gradual conductance modulation. In contrast, devices with relatively
thinner or thicker flakes also display gradual conductance modulation, but their memory
windows in the I-V switching curves are narrower. Accordingly, for the fabrication of the 5×5
device array, we selected a large CBPS nanoflake with a thickness of 22 nm and transferred it
onto the pre-patterned electrode array. This method ensured that all 25 devices within the array
shared the same thickness, orientation, and crystalline quality, avoiding variations that might
arise from using different nanoflakes. The AFM characterization of the CBPS nanoflake
(Figure R16) confirmed that the transferred nanoflake exhibited a smooth surface without
obvious wrinkles or organic residue from the PDMS carrier. In addition, a mild post-transfer
annealing treatment (100 °C, 10 min) was applied to further improvement of the contact quality
between the CBPS nanoflake and the electrodes.

Reply: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the valuable comments. CBPS is a graphene-like
van der Waals layered material. Similar to graphene, the adjacent layers of the CBPS are held
together by weak van der Waals forces. This structural feature enables the mechanical
exfoliation of high-quality, single-crystalline two-dimensional nanoflakes while preserving
their layered order and crystalline integrity. Therefore, the mechanical exfoliation method from
bulk single crystals is a widely adopted and effective way for device fabrication in 2D materials
research.
To ensure the uniform thickness and surface quality of the selected nanoflakes, we first
screened candidate regions using optical microscopy and further confirmed the thickness and
surface flatness using AFM. The AFM images (Figure R16, Figure R19a) showed that the
nanoflake surfaces were smooth and free wrinkles or contaminants, meeting the requirements
for subsequent device fabrication.
During the fabrication of the device arrays, to prevent electrical crosstalk between
neighboring devices, we employed EBL combined with an etching process to define the active
regions of the transferred nanoflakes (Figure R17). This step physically isolates adjacent cells
and ensures that each device operates independently (Figure R19b). During electrical
measurements, each device was tested individually, with probe connections and measurement
setup applied only to the selected device. This fabrication and testing protocol effectively
eliminates potential electrical interference or crosstalk from adjacent devices. We have added

modulation under specific voltage pulse parameters. These functions share the same underlying
origin—Cu⁺ ion displacement–driven polarization switching—which enables dynamic weight
adaptation and threshold sliding analogous to biological synapses without the need for complex
peripheral circuits. Therefore, the synaptic plasticity features such as potentiation/depression,
sliding-threshold learning, and dynamic current responses are not independent effects, but
rather emergent behaviors arising from the intrinsic polarization dynamics induced by Cu⁺ ion
displacement.
